lessonTitle: Mechanisms of Antibiotic Resistance: Enzymes, Altered Targets, Efflux and Spread

blocks.text: A 58-year-old man recovering from a hip replacement has a red, discharging wound. The swab grows Staphylococcus aureus, and the susceptibility report shows it is resistant to flucloxacillin and to every other conventional penicillin and cephalosporin tested, yet fully sensitive to vancomycin. A single genetic change has made a whole drug family useless, and the same genes may already be moving between bacteria on his ward.

blocks.markdown: Resistance can be **intrinsic** (a property of the species, such as Gram-negative bacteria excluding vancomycin) or **acquired** (a previously susceptible strain gains resistance by mutation or by receiving genes). Acquired resistance acts through four main mechanisms: **enzymatic inactivation of the drug**, **alteration of the target**, **reduced intracellular concentration** (efflux pumps or reduced permeability) and **bypass** of the blocked pathway.

blocks.caption: Main mechanisms of resistance
rows: Enzyme destroys or modifies the drug
Beta-lactamases hydrolyse the beta-lactam ring; aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes
Drug target changes so the drug binds poorly
PBP2a in MRSA; D-Ala-D-Lac in vancomycin-resistant enterococci; gyrase mutations for quinolones
Efflux pumps export the drug or porins are lost
Efflux of tetracyclines and macrolides; porin loss in Gram-negative bacteria

blocks.title: Beta-lactamase
blocks.text: A beta-lactamase is an enzyme that hydrolyses the amide bond in the beta-lactam ring of penicillins, cephalosporins and related drugs, producing an inactive product before the drug reaches its penicillin-binding protein target. Gram-positive bacteria usually secrete the enzyme outside the cell; Gram-negative bacteria hold it in the periplasmic space.

blocks.markdown: **Beta-lactamase production.** The ring that mimics D-Ala-D-Ala is the part that binds penicillin-binding proteins; hydrolysis opens that ring and abolishes activity. Genes are often on **plasmids**, so the trait spreads. Different enzymes have different spectra: **extended-spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBLs)** in Enterobacterales hydrolyse penicillins and most cephalosporins; **carbapenemases** also hydrolyse carbapenems. Many beta-lactamases are inhibited by **beta-lactamase inhibitors** (clavulanic acid, tazobactam), which is why an inhibitor combined with a penicillin may restore activity against some producers, although not against all enzymes.

blocks.title: Predicting the effect of a beta-lactamase inhibitor
blocks.prompt: An E. coli isolate is resistant to amoxicillin but susceptible to amoxicillin combined with clavulanic acid. What is the likely mechanism and why does the combination work?

steps.text: Resistance to a penicillin that is reversed by an inhibitor points to a beta-lactamase.
Clavulanic acid binds the enzyme and inactivates it, so amoxicillin survives long enough to reach its penicillin-binding protein target.
The effect would not be expected if resistance were due to altered PBPs or efflux, since the inhibitor does not act on those.

blocks.answer: Beta-lactamase production; the inhibitor protects the penicillin from hydrolysis.

blocks.markdown: **Methicillin resistance in *Staphylococcus aureus* (MRSA).** MRSA carries the gene **mecA**, on a mobile genetic element called the staphylococcal cassette chromosome mec (SCCmec). It encodes **PBP2a**, an altered penicillin-binding protein with **very low affinity** for beta-lactams. When the normal PBPs are inhibited, PBP2a continues to cross-link peptidoglycan, so cell wall synthesis proceeds. The result is resistance to essentially all conventional beta-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins and carbapenems), regardless of beta-lactamase inhibitors, because the mechanism is target alteration not enzymatic destruction. Treatment relies on agents with different targets, such as vancomycin, which binds D-Ala-D-Ala rather than PBPs.

blocks.title: Distinguishing two kinds of staphylococcal resistance
blocks.prompt: Strain X is resistant to benzylpenicillin but sensitive to flucloxacillin. Strain Y is resistant to both. Name the mechanism in each.

steps.text: Strain X: penicillinase (a beta-lactamase) destroys benzylpenicillin, but flucloxacillin is stable to the staphylococcal penicillinase, so it still works.
Strain Y: resistance to flucloxacillin as well means the target is altered: mecA-encoded PBP2a, so Y is MRSA.

blocks.answer: X: staphylococcal beta-lactamase; Y: mecA-mediated PBP2a (MRSA).

blocks.markdown: **Selection pressure and horizontal gene transfer.** Resistance genes arise by **mutation** (rare, random) or are acquired by **horizontal gene transfer**: **conjugation** of plasmids, **transduction** by bacteriophage, **transformation** from free DNA, and movement of genes by **transposons**. Antibiotics do not cause the mutation; they **select** for existing resistant cells. In a large population of susceptible bacteria, a few resistant mutants pre-exist. When the drug is applied, susceptible cells die or stop growing, and the resistant cells multiply and dominate (**selection pressure**). Any exposure, including needless prescribing and agricultural use, increases selection. Plasmids often carry several resistance genes together, so one drug may select for resistance to several (**co-selection**), and the genes can spread to other bacteria and species.

blocks.caption: mu: probability of a resistance mutation per cell; N: number of cells in the population

blocks.title: Pre-existing mutants
blocks.prompt: A culture contains 5 x 10^9 bacteria. The mutation rate to resistance for a drug is 2 x 10^-8 per cell. How many resistant cells are expected before the drug is added?

steps.text: Multiply mutation probability by population size.

blocks.answer: About 100 resistant cells, which are selected when the drug is applied.

items: Four mechanisms: enzyme, altered target, reduced concentration (efflux, porins), bypass.
Beta-lactamase: hydrolyses the beta-lactam ring; inhibitors such as clavulanate may restore activity.
MRSA: mecA, PBP2a, low affinity for beta-lactams.
Antibiotics select, they do not create, resistance.

blocks.title: Selection plus transfer
blocks.text: Resistance spreads because antibiotic use selects for resistant bacteria and mobile genetic elements move resistance genes between organisms. Reducing unnecessary use and preventing cross-infection both reduce spread.

blocks.title: Do not confuse the mechanisms
blocks.text: Adding a beta-lactamase inhibitor does not help against MRSA because the problem is the target (PBP2a), not an enzyme. Antibiotics do not induce mutations in a directed way; they favour cells that already carry resistance.

points: Resistance occurs by enzymatic inactivation, target alteration, efflux or reduced permeability, and bypass.
Beta-lactamases hydrolyse the beta-lactam ring; MRSA instead uses PBP2a encoded by mecA, giving resistance to conventional beta-lactams.
Antibiotics select resistant cells; plasmids, phages, transformation and transposons transfer resistance genes horizontally.

questions.stem: How does a beta-lactamase confer resistance to penicillins?

options.text: It hydrolyses the beta-lactam ring, inactivating the drug
It pumps the drug out of the cell
It alters the ribosome so the drug cannot bind
It blocks uptake through the porin

questions.correctOptionText: It hydrolyses the beta-lactam ring, inactivating the drug

distractorRationale.c: Ribosomal alteration confers resistance to protein synthesis inhibitors.

questions.explanation: Beta-lactamases are enzymes that open the beta-lactam ring, destroying the structure that binds penicillin-binding proteins. The drug is inactivated before it reaches its target.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has a Gram-negative bacteraemia. The isolate is resistant to amoxicillin and to a third-generation cephalosporin, but susceptible to a carbapenem. Which resistance mechanism is most likely?

options.text: Extended-spectrum beta-lactamase production
mecA-mediated PBP2a
D-Ala-D-Lac substitution
Methylation of the 23S ribosomal RNA only

distractorRationale.a: Correct: ESBLs hydrolyse penicillins and cephalosporins but not carbapenems.
distractorRationale.b: PBP2a is found in MRSA, a Gram-positive coccus.
distractorRationale.c: D-Ala-D-Lac causes vancomycin resistance in enterococci.
distractorRationale.d: Ribosomal methylation affects macrolides, not beta-lactams.

questions.explanation: Resistance to penicillins and cephalosporins with retained carbapenem activity is the classic ESBL pattern. Carbapenems are stable to ESBLs, though they are hydrolysed by carbapenemases.

questions.stem: What is the molecular basis of methicillin resistance in Staphylococcus aureus?

options.text: mecA encodes PBP2a, a penicillin-binding protein with low affinity for beta-lactams
A plasmid-borne beta-lactamase that hydrolyses methicillin
Loss of the cell wall, so there is no target
An efflux pump specific to methicillin

questions.correctOptionText: mecA encodes PBP2a, a penicillin-binding protein with low affinity for beta-lactams

distractorRationale.b: A beta-lactamase gives resistance to benzylpenicillin but not typically to methicillin-class drugs.
distractorRationale.c: MRSA has a normal cell wall.
distractorRationale.d: Efflux is not the main mechanism.

questions.explanation: PBP2a continues cross-linking peptidoglycan when other PBPs are blocked. Because the problem is the target, resistance extends to most beta-lactams.

questions.stem: A ward pharmacist proposes treating an MRSA-colonised patient with amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid, arguing that the inhibitor will neutralise the resistance. Why is this unlikely to work?

options.text: Resistance is due to altered PBP2a, not an enzyme, so an enzyme inhibitor does not help
Clavulanic acid is destroyed by the cell wall
Clavulanic acid cannot enter Gram-positive cells
Clavulanic acid binds PBP2a and enhances resistance

questions.correctOptionText: Resistance is due to altered PBP2a, not an enzyme, so an enzyme inhibitor does not help

distractorRationale.b: This is not a recognised effect.
distractorRationale.c: The issue is not entry of the inhibitor.
distractorRationale.d: Clavulanic acid does not enhance resistance.

questions.explanation: Flucloxacillin resistance in S. aureus is due to mecA-encoded PBP2a, which beta-lactamase inhibitors do not affect. Alternative drugs with different targets, such as vancomycin, are required.

questions.stem: Which statement about antibiotic selection pressure is correct?

options.text: Antibiotics eliminate susceptible bacteria and allow pre-existing or acquired resistant bacteria to multiply
Antibiotics direct bacteria to mutate in the needed gene
Resistance can only arise in the infected organ and never in gut flora
Resistance genes can only be passed from parent to daughter cell

questions.correctOptionText: Antibiotics eliminate susceptible bacteria and allow pre-existing or acquired resistant bacteria to multiply

distractorRationale.b: Mutations are random; antibiotics select, not direct them.
distractorRationale.c: Resistance is selected in normal flora too.
distractorRationale.d: Horizontal gene transfer also moves genes between cells.

questions.explanation: Mutations occur randomly and independently of the drug. The antibiotic then provides the environment in which resistant cells outgrow susceptible ones.

questions.stem: A laboratory tests 250 Escherichia coli urinary isolates and finds 45 resistant to an antibiotic. Calculate the percentage of isolates that are resistant.
questions.explanation: Percentage resistant = 45 / 250 x 100 = 18%. Surveillance of such proportions guides local empirical antibiotic choice and monitors the spread of resistance.

questions.stem: A bacterial population contains 4 x 10^10 cells. The mutation rate to resistance for a drug is 5 x 10^-9 per cell. How many resistant mutants are expected before any drug is added (expected number = mutation rate x population)?
questions.explanation: Expected mutants = 5 x 10^-9 x 4 x 10^10 = 200. These cells are selected and multiply when the drug removes susceptible competitors, which is why large populations such as abscesses are prone to resistance.

questions.stem: Explain how beta-lactamase production leads to resistance, and how a beta-lactamase inhibitor such as clavulanic acid can restore activity of amoxicillin.
markingGuide: Drug is inactivated before binding penicillin-binding proteins
Genes are often plasmid-borne and transferable
Clavulanic acid binds and inactivates the enzyme
Inhibitor combination protects amoxicillin; does not work if resistance is due to altered PBPs or some carbapenemases
questions.explanation: The mechanism is enzymatic destruction of the drug. An inhibitor sacrifices itself to the enzyme so the antibiotic can reach its target.

questions.stem: Explain the mechanism of methicillin resistance in Staphylococcus aureus and why it affects almost all beta-lactam antibiotics.
markingGuide: mecA gene on SCCmec mobile element
Encodes PBP2a, a penicillin-binding protein with low affinity for beta-lactams
PBP2a continues cross-linking peptidoglycan when other PBPs are inhibited
Resistance is by target alteration, so conventional penicillins, cephalosporins and carbapenems are affected
Beta-lactamase inhibitors do not help; alternatives such as vancomycin act on a different target
questions.explanation: The target, not an enzyme, has changed, so every drug directed at the usual PBPs fails. This explains why MRSA needs agents with a different mechanism.

questions.stem: Describe how selection pressure and horizontal gene transfer together explain the rapid spread of antibiotic resistance in a hospital.
markingGuide: Resistant mutants or acquired genes pre-exist in large populations
Antibiotics kill susceptible cells and select resistant ones, which multiply (selection pressure)
Horizontal transfer by conjugation (plasmids), transduction, transformation and transposons
Plasmids carry multiple resistance genes causing co-selection
Cross-infection and heavy antibiotic use in hospitals spread and select resistant strains; stewardship and infection control limit this
questions.explanation: Selection increases the proportion of resistant bacteria, and gene transfer spreads resistance between strains and species. Both processes act together in hospital settings.
